polozky.nadpis: How Drone Surveys Expand What’s Surveyable From the Air
polozky.perex: Ten years ago, an aerial survey usually meant a manned aircraft, a mobilisation cost that ruled out anything but the largest jobs.
polozky.telo: Ten years ago, an aerial survey usually meant a manned aircraft, a mobilisation cost that ruled out anything but the largest jobs. Drones changed the economics fast, and most of the conversation since has been about speed: faster mobilisation, faster processing, lower cost per hectare. The bigger shift is what UAV survey platforms have done for sites that were once barely surveyable at all. Reaching What Was Once Off-Limits Until recently, a coastal slope that had just failed, a quarry face still being cut, or a flood-damaged corridor with no stable ground to stand on simply didn’t get surveyed to the same standard as a stable site. polozky.nadpis: Will Gaussian Splatting Replace 3D Textured Meshes?
polozky.perex: Gaussian splatting is rapidly gaining attention as a new way to create highly realistic 3D representations from imagery.
polozky.telo: Gaussian splatting is rapidly gaining attention as a new way to create highly realistic 3D representations from imagery. But beyond impressive visualization, what can Gaussian splats actually be used for in photogrammetry? Join our guest Dr. Jules Morel, Data Analyst at Mirukuru in Japan, as we examine how Gaussian splats are created, what is required to achieve high-quality results, and where the technology fits within real-world photogrammetry workflows. We will also compare Gaussian splats with traditional textured meshes and discuss when each approach makes sense. polozky.telo: From Himalayan rail tunnels to airport drone corridors, the same technology is redefining what reliable positioning means For most of its history, the positioning and mapping industry has measured progress in centimeters. How accurately can you place a point? How tightly can you constrain the error? Accuracy was the ultimate arbiter of a system’s worth and in surveying, engineering and infrastructure, the cost of being wrong is very real. But today, accuracy alone is no longer enough. The environments in which positioning systems operate are more complex, more constrained, and, in some regions, openly challenging to GNSS.
